body.en: Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently, so the cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of life. Anton von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell, and Robert Brown later discovered the nucleus. In 1838 Matthias Schleiden (plants) and in 1839 Theodore Schwann (animals) proposed that living bodies are made of cells; Schwann also noted the plasma membrane and that the cell wall is unique to plant cells. In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that new cells arise from pre-existing cells: Omnis cellula-e cellula.

points.en: All living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells.
All cells arise from pre-existing cells (Virchow, 1855).
Schleiden and Schwann could not explain how new cells are formed.

narration.en: Let us build the cell theory on a timeline and compare the two kinds of cells.

say.en: Schleiden studied plants in 1838 and Schwann studied animals in 1839. Both found that living things are made of cells.
In 1855 Virchow added the missing piece: every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.
Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane: their DNA lies naked in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.
Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Ribosomes occur in both kinds.
Cells vary hugely in size: Mycoplasma is only 0.3 micrometre, bacteria 3 to 5, a human red blood cell about 7 micrometres.
Let us build the cell theory on a timeline and compare the two kinds of cells.

narration.en: Cell theory was built step by step by several scientists. Arrange their work in order.

prompt.en: Put these discoveries in the order they happened.

steps.en: Anton van Leeuwenhoek first sees and describes a live cell
Matthias Schleiden: all plants are made of different kinds of cells (1838)
Theodore Schwann: animal cells have a thin outer layer, the plasma membrane; plants and animals are made of cells (1839)
Rudolf Virchow: all cells arise from pre-existing cells (1855)

explanation.en: Schleiden and Schwann together proposed the cell theory, but it did not explain how new cells form. Virchow added "Omnis cellula-e cellula", giving the cell theory its final form.

say.en: Cell theory was built step by step by several scientists. Arrange their work in order.

body.en: Every cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm (the main arena of cell activity) and ribosomes. Eukaryotic *cells* have a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; prokaryotic cells have neither. Cells vary greatly: Mycoplasma is the smallest cell (about 0.3 μm), bacteria are 3–5 μm, a human red blood cell is about 7.0 μm across, nerve cells are among the longest, and the egg of an ostrich is the largest isolated single cell.

points.en: Ribosomes are present in all *cells*, inside and outside organelles.
Plant *cells* have a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole; animal cells have centrioles.
Cell shape suits function: disc-shaped RBCs, branched nerve *cells*, columnar epithelium.

problem.en: Arrange these cells from smallest to largest: human RBC, Mycoplasma, a typical bacterium, ostrich egg.

steps.en: Mycoplasma is about 0.3 μm, the smallest known cell.
A typical bacterium is 3–5 μm; a human RBC is about 7 μm across.
The ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell.

say.en: Let us work through this together. Arrange these cells from smallest to largest: human RBC, Mycoplasma, a typical bacterium, ostrich egg.
Mycoplasma is about 0.3 micrometres, the smallest known cell.
A typical bacterium is 3-5 micrometres; a human RBC is about 7 micrometres across.
The ostrich egg is the largest isolated single cell.
So the answer is Mycoplasma is less than bacterium is less than human RBC is less than ostrich egg.
